choices: We loaded the van with tents sleeping bags and a folding table.
We loaded the van with tents, sleeping bags, and a folding table.
We loaded, the van with tents, sleeping bags and a folding table.
We loaded the van, with tents sleeping bags, and a folding table.
hints: Three or more items in a row form a series, and a series needs commas between the items.
Put a comma after each item except the last, keep the comma before "and", and never drop a comma between a verb and its object.

choices: After the last bell rang the hallway emptied in under a minute.
After the last bell rang, the hallway, emptied in under a minute.
After the last bell rang, the hallway emptied in under a minute.
After, the last bell rang the hallway emptied in under a minute.
hints: Find where the setup ends and the main subject begins.
An introductory element closes with a comma, and nothing may sit between the subject "the hallway" and its verb "emptied".

choices: The freezer stopped working overnight, and the ice cream turned to soup.
The freezer stopped working overnight and the ice cream turned to soup.
The freezer stopped working overnight, the ice cream turned to soup.
The freezer stopped working, and turned the ice cream to soup.
hints: Read the words on each side of "and" alone. Could each half stand as its own complete sentence?
Two independent clauses joined by a conjunction take a comma BEFORE the conjunction; a comma with no conjunction leaves two sentences taped together.

choices: Our neighbor, a retired ferry captain sharpens every knife on the block.
Our neighbor a retired ferry captain, sharpens every knife on the block.
Our neighbor, a retired ferry captain, sharpens every knife, on the block.
Our neighbor, a retired ferry captain, sharpens every knife on the block.
hints: Lift out "a retired ferry captain" and reread. Does the sentence still work and still mean the same person?
Nonessential information takes a PAIR of commas, one before and one after; a single comma builds half a fence, and no comma job exists between a verb and its object.

choices: A cold, steady rain fell on the three old wooden crates by the door.
A cold steady rain fell on the three, old, wooden crates by the door.
A cold, steady rain fell on the three, old wooden crates by the door.
A cold steady rain fell on the three old wooden crates, by the door.
hints: Test each pair of adjectives twice: put "and" between them, then reverse their order.
"Cold and steady" and "steady, cold" both work, so those two are coordinate and take a comma. "Three old wooden" fails both tests, so it takes none.

choices: After the power flickered twice the projector, which had never been serviced, shut down, and refused to restart.
After the power flickered twice, the projector, which had never been serviced, shut down and refused to restart.
After the power flickered twice, the projector which had never been serviced, shut down and refused to restart.
After the power flickered twice, the projector, which had never been serviced shut down, and refused to restart.
hints: Three decisions are stacked here: the introductory element, the interrupting clause, and whatever sits before "and".
The opener needs a closing comma, the deletable clause needs a comma on BOTH sides, and "refused to restart" has no subject of its own, so it is a compound verb and takes no comma before "and".

problemText: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
choices: Because the elevator was out of service; we carried every box up four flights.
The elevator was out of service; and we carried every box up four flights.
The elevator was out of service; we carried every box up four flights.
The elevator was out of service; carrying every box up four flights.
hints: Cover each side of the semicolon in turn and read it aloud on its own.
A semicolon needs a complete sentence on BOTH sides, and it is never followed directly by and, but, or so.

problemText: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
choices: The packing list included: a rain jacket, sturdy boots, and a water bottle.
The packing list included three things: a rain jacket, sturdy boots, and a water bottle.
The three things on the packing list were: a rain jacket, sturdy boots, and a water bottle.
The packing list included items such as: a rain jacket, sturdy boots, and a water bottle.
hints: Cover the list in each choice and read only the words in front of the colon.
A colon demands a complete independent clause on its left. Endings like "included", "were", and "such as" leave the clause unfinished.

choices: The recipe doubled easily, therefore, we made enough for the whole hall.
The recipe doubled easily therefore; we made enough for the whole hall.
The recipe doubled easily: therefore we made enough for the whole hall.
The recipe doubled easily; therefore, we made enough for the whole hall.
hints: "Therefore" is a transition word, not a conjunction like and or but, so it cannot hold two complete sentences together by itself.
When a transition word opens the second complete sentence, the semicolon goes BEFORE it and a comma goes AFTER it.

choices: Three cousins signed the card: Marisol, who lives two towns over; Dev, who moved last spring; and Ana, who could not attend.
Three cousins signed the card: Marisol, who lives two towns over, Dev, who moved last spring, and Ana, who could not attend.
Three cousins signed the card; Marisol, who lives two towns over; Dev, who moved last spring; and Ana, who could not attend.
Three cousins signed the card: Marisol, who lives two towns over; Dev, who moved last spring, and Ana, who could not attend.
hints: Each item in this list already contains a comma of its own, which makes ordinary commas useless as dividers.
Upgrade the dividers between items to semicolons and keep the colon after the complete clause that introduces them. Every divider in the list must be the same mark.

choices: One detail gave the forgery away; the signature spelled two different ways.
One detail gave the forgery away, the signature was spelled two different ways.
One detail gave the forgery away: the signature was spelled two different ways.
One detail gave the forgery away; because the signature was spelled two different ways.
hints: The first half promises a detail without naming it, and the second half delivers exactly that detail.
A colon points forward from a complete clause to the explanation it promised. A semicolon still needs a full sentence after it, and a comma alone cannot join two sentences.

choices: We rewired the whole booth on Saturday; however, hoping the sound check would go faster on Sunday.
We rewired the whole booth on Saturday, hoping the sound check would go faster on Sunday; it did not.
We rewired the whole booth on Saturday; hoping the sound check would go faster on Sunday, it did not.
We rewired the whole booth on Saturday: hoping the sound check would go faster on Sunday; it did not.
hints: Isolate "hoping the sound check would go faster on Sunday" and ask whether it has a subject and a main verb.
It is a fragment, so it attaches to the clause before it with a comma. The only place a semicolon earns its keep here is in front of "it did not", which is a complete sentence.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "The old radio lost ___ antenna years ago."
choices: it's
its
its'
it is
hints: Expand the apostrophe form: does "the old radio lost it is antenna" read correctly?
The antenna belongs to the radio, so this slot needs the possessive pronoun, and possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

problemText: Three swimmers share a row of lockers. Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "The three ___ lockers were repainted over the break."
choices: swimmers
swimmer's
swimmers'
swimmers's
hints: Flip the phrase with "of": the lockers OF the swimmers. Ownership is real here, and the owner is plural.
Pluralize first, then punctuate. A regular plural already ends in -s, so it takes an apostrophe alone with nothing after it.

choices: The bakery sells four kinds of muffin's before noon.
The bakery sell's four kinds of muffins before noon.
The bakery sells four kind's of muffin's before noon.
The bakery sells four kinds of muffins before noon.
hints: Ask of every apostrophe you see: what does this word own, or what letters are missing?
Nothing belongs to the muffins and no letters have been dropped, so these are plain plurals and take no apostrophe at all.

choices: The childrens' choir rehearses in the room whose windows face the courtyard.
The children's choir rehearses in the room whose windows face the courtyard.
The children's choir rehearses in the room who's windows face the courtyard.
The childrens's choir rehearses in the room who's windows face the courtyard.
hints: "Children" is already the plural, and it does not end in -s. Also expand "who's" and see whether "who is windows" survives.
Plurals that do not end in -s take a normal apostrophe plus s, and the possessive form before "windows" is "whose".

problemText: Which choice correctly fills the two blanks, in order? "The seniors left ___ props backstage because ___ repainting the set tomorrow."
choices: they're ... their
their ... their
their ... they're
there ... their
hints: Try expanding "they are" into each blank one at a time.
Blank one shows props belonging to the seniors, so it takes the possessive. Blank two means "they are repainting the set tomorrow," so it takes the contraction.

choices: The class's banner hung over two rows of trophies, and it's obvious that nobody had dusted them since June.
The class' banner hung over two rows of trophie's, and its obvious that nobody had dusted them since June.
The classes banner hung over two rows of trophies, and its obvious that nobody had dusted them since June.
The class's banner hung over two rows of trophy's, and its' obvious that nobody had dusted them since June.
hints: Three separate decisions hide in this sentence: the possessive of a singular word that already ends in -s, a plain plural, and a contraction.
One class owns the banner, so it takes apostrophe plus s; the trophies own nothing, so they take no mark; and "it is obvious" expands correctly, so that slot needs the contraction.

choices: The back gate — rusted shut since winter, finally opened on the third try.
The back gate, rusted shut since winter — finally opened on the third try.
The back gate — rusted shut since winter — finally opened on the third try.
The back gate — rusted shut since winter finally opened on the third try.
hints: Delete "rusted shut since winter" and reread. The sentence still works, so the phrase needs a fence on both sides.
Whatever mark opens the aside must close it. A dash opens and a dash closes; a dash paired with a comma is a mixed fence.

choices: Mateo said, "The keys are under the mat."
Mateo said "The keys are under the mat".
Mateo said, "the keys are under the mat".
Mateo said. "The keys are under the mat."
hints: Check three things: the mark joining the speech tag to the quotation, the capital letter, and where the closing period sits.
A comma joins a speech tag to quoted words, the first word of a quoted sentence is capitalized, and in American usage the period goes INSIDE the closing quotation mark.

choices: The recycling bins (which the custodians empty on Tuesdays, sit behind the cafeteria.
The recycling bins (which the custodians empty on Tuesdays) sit behind the cafeteria.
The recycling bins (which the custodians empty on Tuesdays.) sit behind the cafeteria
The recycling bins, which the custodians empty on Tuesdays) sit behind the cafeteria.
hints: An opening parenthesis can only be closed by its partner, never by a comma.
Remove the parenthetical entirely and the sentence outside it must still read correctly and still end with its own period.

problemText: Which sentence uses a single dash correctly?
choices: We searched — the attic for two hours and came away with a cracked ornament.
We searched the attic for two hours and came away with — a cracked ornament.
We searched the attic — for two hours and came away with a cracked ornament.
We searched the attic for two hours and came away with a single item — a cracked ornament.
hints: Cover everything from the dash onward in each choice. Can the words before the dash stand alone as a complete sentence?

A single emphatic dash breaks AFTER a complete clause and then delivers the punch. Dropping it between a verb and its object, or between a preposition and its object, cuts the sentence in the wrong place.

problemText: A character is repeating what someone else told her. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: 'Coach kept shouting "reset the line," so we reset it,' Devon told me.
"Coach kept shouting 'reset the line,' so we reset it," Devon told me.
"Coach kept shouting 'reset the line', so we reset it", Devon told me.
"Coach kept shouting 'reset the line,' so we reset it", Devon told me.
hints: Decide which marks hold the outer speech and which hold the quotation buried inside it.
The outer quotation takes double marks and the inner one takes single marks, and every comma or period that ends quoted words sits INSIDE the quotation mark that closes them.

choices: The sign taped to the register (hand-lettered and already peeling) warned customers, "Cash only today."
The sign taped to the register (hand-lettered and already peeling, warned customers, "Cash only today".
The sign taped to the register — hand-lettered and already peeling) warned customers, "Cash only today."
The sign taped to the register, hand-lettered and already peeling — warned customers, "cash only today".
hints: Two problems are stacked here: the fence around the aside, and the punctuation of the quoted words at the end.
The fence must open and close with the SAME mark, the first word of the quoted sentence is capitalized, and the final period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.
